entry.title: A relook at food subsidy
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / A relook at food subsidyA relook at food subsidy

Estimates on poverty reduction should be used to usher in a targeted scheme for free foodgrain

premium

Illustration: Ajaya Kumar Mohanty

A K Bhattacharya New Delhi 6 min read Last Updated : Nov 03 2026 | 10:27 PM ISTLess than three months are left before the Union Budget for 2027-28 is due to be presented in Parliament. Even as inter-ministerial consultations have started and discussions with representatives of industry, trade, and farmers, among others, are set to be held soon, expectations from the forthcoming Budget are already running high. This is not just because the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) has called for the removal of the long-term capital gains tax for foreign portfolio investors, but also because Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman has responded to this issue by making a careful statement that the government acknowledges concerns about sustained foreign investment inflows and the market’s anxiety over them.  Expectedly, the stock market has responded positively to these statements in the hope that the Union Budget on February 1 will revise the taxation framework for long-term capital gains from assets. At another level, senior government officials are making statements that underline the need for more reforms. Those too have raised expectations from the forthcoming Budget.  Last week, Chief Economic Advisor (CEA) V Anantha Nageswaran delivered an important address highlighting the imperatives before India’s economic policymakers in the face of the current challenges. For obvious reasons, the headline for the CEA’s address focused on the comparison between the current economic challenges of 2026 and those that India faced in 1991. Of course, the comparison was qualified, even though the structural and external challenges were as formidable then as they are now. The policy suggestions made by the CEA, particularly the one requiring a re-examination of the country’s growth and industrial strategies, deserve serious consideration. The simultaneous pursuit of import substitution, stronger local manufacturing, and improved export competitiveness will also require a reimagined policy approach.  Similarly, recent statements from Niti Aayog Member Rajiv Gauba have ignited hopes of an overhaul of urban governance, with empowered city governments, directly elected mayors with five-year terms, greater financial autonomy for urban local bodies, and the introduction of integrated land-use planning in cities and towns of India. Over the past many years, the Union Budget has gone beyond fiscal matters, outlining the government’s overall development policies as well. Mr Gauba’s statement that urban centres cannot be effectively run from state Capitals should lead to necessary governance reforms, as city governments will require the authority, resources and institutional capacity to address local developmental issues.  The coming Union Budget can lay down a road map for ensuring the devolvement of all 18 functions, listed under the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act to urban local bodies. States can be nudged to ensure that urban local bodies are empowered to take decisions on master planning, water supply, fire services, and traffic management, which are all functions currently controlled by most state governments.  But going beyond governance, there is an important issue that the Union Budget should tackle to support the government’s fiscal situation. That reform should be in the area of food subsidies and its need has been triggered by a World Bank report (the Poverty and Equity Brief for India) released in October. It states that between 2011 and 2023, the share of Indians living below the poverty line, using the yardstick for lower middle-income countries (daily consumption of $4.2), fell from 57.7 per cent to 16.1 per cent. The World Bank report released another datapoint indicating that India’s extreme poverty (measured by a daily consumption of $3, used for low-income countries) fell from 27.1 per cent to 2.6 per cent during the same period. But the relevant number for India’s poverty estimate is the one showing the decline in the share of poor people in the country’s total population to 16.1 per cent. India is a lower middle-income country and the daily consumption benchmark of $4.2 is the correct yardstick to measure India’s poverty level.  Such a reduction in India’s poverty level is obviously being debated among economists. There are many questions about how this reduction was achieved and whether it impacted the level of inequality in India. While these issues warrant further discussion, another policy debate should be triggered by this poverty reduction. This is about the Modi government’s scheme to supply free foodgrain to over 800 million Indians.  Remember that India did not have a free foodgrain scheme in 2011, when its poverty level was 57.7 per cent, according to the World Bank. The free foodgrain scheme was started in March 2020 in response to the Covid pandemic. It was tweaked slightly to cover all beneficiaries under the National Food Security Act in January 2023 for a period of 12 months, even though Covid was no longer a threat at that time. Then, a few weeks before January 2024, it was announced that the free foodgrain scheme would run for five years. In the process, over 57 per cent of India’ total population has come to enjoy free foodgrain, even though the country has a poverty rate of 16 per cent.  For the Union government, the free foodgrain scheme entails a significant cost. Food subsidies are estimated at over ₹2 trillion every year, over four per cent of the government’s total annual expenditure. Food subsidies cannot be completely eliminated. But they can certainly be reduced significantly if the free foodgrain scheme is targeted to benefit only the poor. Any such move will face obvious political pushback because of the electoral costs it could impose on the ruling party.  But a government that could take on powerful retailers by reintroducing the merchant discount rate (MDR) on select transactions made through the Unified Payments Interface can be expected to roll out a similar free foodgrain scheme that benefits only the poor and needy.  Why talk of only traders? The government this year has successfully linked the sale of fertilisers to farmers’ land records through the use of AgriStack and other digital platforms. Fertiliser sales this kharif season fell by over 37 per cent. As a result, the new scheme has prevented large-scale diversion of fertilisers to non-farming sectors and to neighbouring countries, where fertiliser prices are much higher. The government’s fertiliser subsidies bill too has benefitted.  Hopefully, the proposed MDR will be enforced after Diwali, and the scheme linking fertiliser sales to land records will be continued and expanded to cover more farmers after addressing concerns of tenant farmers. Food and fertiliser subsidies in the first half of the current financial year have been kept under check so far, growing by 13 per cent against the annual growth projection of 18 per cent. Given the way energy prices have been behaving, the government needs to introduce these subsidy reforms to provide some cushion against expenditure slippages in other areas this year and during 2027-28.     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: India can't afford to ignore money growth
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India can't afford to ignore money growthIndia can't afford to ignore money growth

With inflation expectations difficult to measure in India's context, monetary aggregates offer a valuable cross-check

premium

Reserve bank of India (Photo: Reuters)

Prasanna Tantri5 min read Last Updated : Nov 03 2026 | 10:34 PM IST“Similarly, there are risks of demand-side pressures in view of the growth in monetary and credit aggregates.” This sentence from the Reserve Bank of India Governor in the latest Monetary Policy Committee minutes deserves attention. After receding from public-policy discussions, the quantity of money is receiving explicit recognition once again. Should we bother with it when the RBI already sets interest rates and targets inflation? In India, the answer is yes.  The numbers explain why. Broad money, or M3, consists principally of currency and bank deposits. Its growth accelerated from around 9.3 per cent in 2024-25 to 15.3 per cent in 2025-26, while nominal gross domestic product (GDP) grew by less than 9 per cent in the latter year. Annual money growth remained at 16 per cent on October 15. Our compilation places M3 at approximately 91 per cent of GDP in March and around 93 per cent by September, using projected GDP. The ratio was approximately 86 per cent 18 months earlier. This represents substantial monetary expansion relative to income.  There is, however, a serious intellectual argument against assigning money growth an independent role in policymaking. In the New Keynesian framework associated with the recent Nobel prize winners, spending responds to current and expected future real interest rates. The relevant real rate is the nominal rate minus expected inflation. Lower real rates encourage spending today and weaken the incentive to postpone consumption. When prices adjust slowly, stronger demand eventually pushes up inflation.  From this perspective, monetary policy works through interest rates, expectations, and financing conditions. The central bank need not separately target money if these channels adequately capture the stance. Money may expand because banks lend more and create deposits, making it partly an outcome of economic decisions rather than an independent cause. Financial innovation also makes money difficult to define, while the central bank cannot precisely control broad money.  Moreover, creating bank reserves does not guarantee additional lending. Banks may retain liquid assets because they fear losses, lack capital or cannot find creditworthy customers. Borrowers may prefer repayment to fresh borrowing. The American experience after the global financial crisis illustrates why reserve creation need not translate proportionately into money, credit or inflation.  Monetarists would respond that this places too much confidence in policymakers’ ability to identify the correct interest rate. A nominal rate can look restrictive while being expansionary once expected inflation is factored in. Sustained growth in money beyond the public’s willingness to hold it encourages adjustment through spending and purchases of assets. Money, therefore, provides information that an interest-rate diagnosis can miss. The relationship is neither immediate nor mechanically proportional: Desired money holdings and the speed of spending also change.  India has two reasons to take this monetarist warning seriously.  First, the possibility that additional liquidity remains disconnected from lending is less reassuring when credit is already expanding strongly. Bank credit reached ₹227.43 trillion on October 15, growing 18.2 per cent over the preceding year, compared with 11.6 per cent a year earlier. This does not establish that reserve creation caused every additional loan. It establishes that we are not observing abundant reserves alongside stagnant bank lending. Money and credit are expanding together.  Second, and more importantly, India lacks a sufficiently reliable measure of the inflation expectations driving spending, saving and price-setting. Household survey expectations persistently exceed subsequent national consumer price index-based inflation. Some discrepancy reflects households’ different consumption baskets. Survey movements can still be informative. But using these numerical expectations to calculate the real rate remains problematic.  Professional forecasts help predict reported inflation, but they cannot substitute for understanding the expectations governing wage negotiations, rents, school fees and contract renewals. Those decisions determine how anticipated inflation enters future prices. We need better surveys and evidence from contracts committing parties to future payments.  Until then, monetary aggregates offer a valuable cross-check. Even someone convinced that money has no independent causal role should ask whether its growth improves inflation forecasts. Prediction does not require establishing that the predictor independently causes the outcome. If money growth helps anticipate inflation, ignoring it because causality is disputed would discard useful information.  This is compatible with a New Keynesian framework. If expected inflation is mismeasured, our estimate of the real rate is wrong. Rapid monetary and credit growth should prompt a reassessment: Is policy providing more stimulus than the nominal repo rate suggests?  Nor is all monetary growth dangerous. A growing economy needs more money, and financial deepening can justify a higher money-to-GDP ratio. The warning is persistent, substantial expansion beyond income growth without evidence of a corresponding increase in desired money holdings.  India’s historical experience suggests that 80-84 per cent of GDP is a useful reference range for broad money, not a scientifically established optimum. Returning towards it gradually would require money growth to lag nominal income growth, rather than an abrupt monetary contraction.  The repo rate should remain the principal instrument and inflation the objective. But money growth deserves an explicit place in forecasts, minutes and communication. When expectations are poorly measured, an interest-rate framework needs more cross-checks, not fewer.

entry.title: COP31 and the world's 35x35 plan
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / COP31 and the world's 35x35 planCOP31 and the world's 35x35 plan

Raising electricity's share in energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035 may look attractive. But is it the right ambition for India?

premium

Solar and wind energy capacity is expanding as India works towards a cleaner electricity mix and its climate goals (Photo: Shutterstock)

R R Rashmi5 min read Last Updated : Nov 02 2026 | 10:48 PM ISTThe next United Nations-mandated climate conference, to be held this month in Antalya, will begin on an anxious note.  The latest Emissions Gap Report 2026 of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) confirms that global emissions have reached a record high of 58 gigatonnes in 2025 and are still rising. Even if all new Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) promised by countries are fully implemented, global emissions will fall by a mere 5-8 per cent by 2030, compared with the 2025 level. For a pathway consistent with the 1.5-degree climate goal, global emissions need to fall by over 43 per cent compared with 2019 levels and 18 per cent compared with 2025 levels. The scenario is, therefore, grim.  Given that NDCs were revised only last year and no further negotiations on the new set of NDCs are on the cards until the next global stocktake in 2028, can the Conference of the Parties (COP31) do anything to buck this trend? More specifically, will India be adversely affected by any action that it may consider?  One such idea that is doing the rounds in anticipation of COP31 is raising the share of electricity in global energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035.  The goal looks attractive and benign because electrification powered by renewables can help reduce emissions significantly. The current global electrification level reported by the International Energy Agency (IEA) is 23 per cent. Moreover, the share of renewable energy, excluding nuclear, in the global electricity generation mix is nearly 34 per cent, and, in terms of capacity, still higher at 49.5 per cent. So, the goal appears to be within reach.  However, there is more to it than meets the eye. Both electrification and renewable energy capacity additions vary widely at global and national levels. In India, for example, electricity’s share of final energy consumption is around 23 per cent. Similarly, the share of renewable energy in the electricity generation mix is around 26 per cent, including large hydro, though its share in terms of overall capacity has risen to over 50 per cent.  As admitted by the International Renewable Energy Agency, the share of renewable energy in the electricity generation mix consistently lags the share of renewable energy in capacity because of lower capacity factors of solar and wind. Rapidly increasing energy demand relative to supply further widens this gap in countries like India. Even in developing economies where the variable cost of solar and wind energy has fallen below that of coal-fired electricity, coal continues to meet over 70 per cent of the final energy consumption because of this reason.  Given this reality, how should India look at the 35x35 electricity goal? A suitable response may depend on four factors.  One, electricity’s share of final energy consumption is contingent upon how energy demand is met in the future. Demand for energy originates not only in the power sector, where renewable energy is dominant, but also in industry and the transport sector, where fossil fuels rule the roost. Electricity growth in these sectors will depend on how quickly and to what extent alternative technologies and fuels, such as green hydrogen, biofuels and electric batteries, can be introduced.  Two, India’s economic growth requires an increase in energy consumption, 72 per cent of which is currently met by fossil fuels. Under the existing policy scenario, electricity’s share in India’s energy consumption may rise to about 24 per cent by 2035, but a further rise may not be linear until India’s emissions peak. This would depend on the dynamics of Viksit Bharat and cannot be predicted with certainty at this stage.  Three, even in the power sector, where renewable energy is rising in the generation mix, further growth is dependent on critical investments in transmission and energy storage. Investments in renewable energy have no doubt accelerated since 2023, when about 120 countries pledged to triple renewable energy capacity. But global capacity is still half of the projected goal of 11,000 Gw by 2030, mainly because transmission and storage have not kept pace.  Four, neither electrification nor renewable energy can expand in the energy system in the absence of dedicated and planned public and private investments in renewable energy infrastructure. Current attention is focused on capacity creation and not on the development of energy storage infrastructure or alternative fuels at scale. Global green finance, being risk-averse and aligned with fossil fuel phase-out policies, is not a reliable partner for planned investments of this nature.  As India is largely dependent on domestic resources to finance the transformation of critical energy infrastructure, it must decide on the pace of its transformation in a manner consistent with the goals of Viksit Bharat and net zero. Raising the share of renewable energy in the electricity generation mix could be a more pragmatic near-term goal than raising electrification’s share in energy consumption.
The writer is distinguished fellow at Teri and a former climate negotiator     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: India's grid-scale moment
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India's grid-scale momentIndia's grid-scale moment

Batteries will power the future economy. India must seize the opportunity to build a globally competitive industry that goes beyond lithium-ion

premium

Illustration: Ajaya Mohanty

Laveesh Bhandari6 min read Last Updated : Nov 02 2026 | 10:38 PM ISTIndia’s energy demand is growing at about the same rate as its gross domestic product or GDP. If the economy becomes five to six times its current size in another 20 years, so will the energy demand. Moreover, electricity will power the bulk of economic activity in the country. As a result, massive power-generation capacity will need to come up in the very near future.  It is also true that renewable energy, specifically wind and solar, is a very cheap source of power.  They will also become cheaper over time. However, they supply electricity intermittently, while power demand is volatile. This is a key problem for utilities or electricity distribution companies.    To match intermittent supply with volatile demand requires some form of electricity storage that can be drawn at will. The scales would be massive and the storage needs will be large as well.  Fortunately, many technological alternatives exist that can help meet such demand-supply gaps. But water, compressed air, and brine-based energy storage solutions are difficult to scale-up.  And, the most used alternative, the lithium-ion battery, is controlled by China and will continue to be for the next five to 10 years.    Each energy storage system has a different set of advantages. While their use is increasing, they are not currently used at scale. If they could be produced at scale, their costs would be significantly lower. Moreover, typically larger setups are better able to attract resources for research and innovation.  And, therefore, India has a great opportunity and challenge for industrial policy on utility-scale power storage. India could do either of three things. The first is to be agnostic to the technology and support any type of battery-based storage.  Roughly, this is what India does currently. The second is to reverse industrial policy, and actively dissuade lithium-ion batteries, letting the industry decide on other alternatives. And the third is to choose a specific type of battery and direct investments towards it.  While technological agnosticism is generally a superior policy solution, focusing on lithium-ion batteries will mean dependence on China for the next decade or so, if not more. India thus needs a policy that seeks to catalyse a new battery industry.  A successful industrial policy for grid-scale storage would, therefore, have three elements. One, it would specify what it is trying to prevent; in this case, it would be lithium-ion. Two, it would seek to promote other technologies. In this, it may specify sodium-ion batteries or be agnostic. And three, it would ensure that an enabling ecosystem is created for new technologies — both financial and regulatory constraints, if any, need to be addressed.   The first step in any policy change is to identify the objective. India’s grid storage mission must adopt an approach that is not just China-resilient but one aimed at harnessing global opportunity. A large market in battery-based storage is opening up not only in India but globally. Just as India is electrifying at a fast pace, so are most other economies, and all have the same needs currently mostly being met by China. Therefore, India needs to think of an alternative that could help it access the global energy-storage market. This market is not just about batteries for achieving energy transition, but also to power the large data centres that need seamless electricity supply.     The second step would be to promote demand for non-lithium grid-storage batteries. And it is here that policymakers will need to better understand industry compulsions. No other battery has been around for a long time, and therefore many parameters, degradation rates, lifespans, efficiency levels are not as well understood for new technologies as they are for lithium-ion batteries.  Left to itself, the market will tend to prefer the well-known technology to new unknown ones.  Recall that the government tried to catalyse India’s renewable energy transition by mandating discoms to purchase renewable energy. A similar mandate, of say a minimum of a quarter of total energy storage using non-lithium storage, would help create early demand for other forms of batteries. This would need to be expanded over time.  Third, the world, including India, has underinvested in the development of sodium-ion batteries, one of the most likely alternatives to lithium-ion.  These batteries have several advantages: Key inputs are mostly available in India, are low-cost when produced at scale, they are environmentally less harmful, and less susceptible to overheating, among others. Currently, they are marginally less efficient and costlier than lithium-ion batteries, but scale should help cover some of the ever-narrowing gap between sodium-ion and lithium   batteries. India has some ongoing initiatives and pilots, but more is required. A great opportunity lies ahead if India can crack the sodium-ion battery ecosystem.     Fourth, the current production-linked incentive (PLI) scheme for battery storage aims to incentivise domestic and global companies to set up giga-scale Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) manufacturing and battery storage facilities in India. As mentioned before, it is technology-agnostic. A variant of the same scheme that focuses on non-lithium grid-scale storage needs to be created that rewards domestic alternatives on the basis of domestic value addition rather than being output-based. As soon as domestic value added enters the PLI equation, lithium becomes less attractive an option.  Fifth, an ecosystem approach is critical for kickstarting a whole new industry. Financial institutions such as the Small Industries Development Bank of India  and the Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Ltd can provide greater support or better terms to utility-scale storage that has a high level of domestic value addition.  Greater research & development allocations, especially in upstream technologies, such as anode and cathodes, would help. Startups in this space can be funded out of various government schemes.  These could be further enabled by capex grants for both incumbents and new entrants. At the same time, a relook at the regulations would help. Many hazmat rules that apply to storage and transport of batteries, among others, currently appear to be designed for lithium-ion batteries, which would need to be corrected.  The larger point being made is that batteries lie at the heart of the future economy, and it would be a good idea to take the driver’s seat on this opportunity.  
 The writer heads the Centre for Social and Economic Progress. The views are personal   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: CGST rule 96(10): Govt must return recovered money
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / CGST rule 96(10): Govt must return recovered moneyCGST rule 96(10): Govt must return recovered money

CBIC's retrospective omission of CGST Rule 96(10) raises questions over amounts recovered from exporters, with the government urged to return refunds and interest collected under the provision

premium

The retrospective omission of CGST Rule 96(10) has prompted exporters to seek the return of GST refunds and interest recovered under the provision.

TNC Rajagopalan Mumbai 3 min read Last Updated : Nov 01 2026 | 11:47 PM ISTLast week, the government issued several notifications and circulars giving effect to the recommendations of theGoods and Services Tax (GST) Council following its 57th meeting in Delhi on October 8, 2026. The recommendations have been discussed at length in the media. So, I will deal with Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) Circular 264/10/2026-GST dated October 26, concerning GST refunds on exports.  Rule 96(10) of the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Rules, 2017 operated with effect from October 23, 2017. In essence, it restricted refunds of Integrated Goods and Services Tax (IGST) paid on exports where specified exemptions or concessions had been availed on imports or domestic procurements. The provision underwent several amendments and generated extensive litigation and demands for surrender of export refunds with interest. Many exporters repaid the amounts under departmental pressure. The government eventually omitted the rule through notification 20/2024 Central Tax dated October 8, 2024. However, this notification contained no saving clause preserving proceedings relating to the period when the rule was in force.  In Goodluck India Ltd. v. Union of India (2026 [112] GSTL 3 [SC]), the Supreme Court considered whether pending proceedings could survive that omission. Relying on the Constitution Bench judgment in Kolhapur Canesugar Works (2000 [119] ELT 257 [SC]), it held that continuation of pending proceedings required an appropriate legal provision preserving them. There was none. The Court said that the GST council’s recommendation for prospective omission of Rule 96(10) could not substitute for a saving clause in the notification. It also noted the council’s assessment that the rule was causing unnecessary complications without serving the intended benefit. The Court saw the omission without a saving clause as intended to end those complications. The judgment, however, must be read accurately. The Supreme Court settled the treatment of pending proceedings but did not declare Rule 96(10) unconstitutional or expressly order reopening of every concluded case.  Now, the CBIC circular says that the omission of Rule 96(10) is effective retrospectively from October 23, 2017, the date from which the rule operated. It advises field formations to deal with pending proceedings concerning Rule 96(10) in accordance with the judgment. It says that similar treatment applies, mutatis mutandis, to the omission of Rules 89(4A) and 89(4B) as well.   Exporters who did not litigate but surrendered refunds along with interest are wondering whether they can ask the government to return the money. If, on the Board’s own interpretation, the omission operates from the rule’s inception, why should the government retain amounts recovered solely under that rule? That is their question.  Statutory refund deadlines and the finality of earlier orders may present legal obstacles to refund claims. The circular alone should not be assumed to remove them. The government should, suo motu, initiate repayment of amounts recovered towards reversal of GST refunds, together with interest collected, wherever the omitted Rule 96(10),   Rule 89(4A) or Rule 89(4B) was the sole basis of recovery. Exporters should not have to apply afresh and litigate again. The department already has records of these recoveries and should identify the affected exporters, verify the amounts collected and arrange repayment without waiting for each exporter to initiate proceedings. Any legal obstacles should be addressed through an appropriate legal mechanism and a simple verification procedure.   Returning these collections would release exporters’ working capital and give practical effect to the Board’s declared position. Closing pending demands while retaining earlier collections would leave the relief incomplete.      Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Yes, blame the state
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Yes, blame the stateYes, blame the state

From sanitation and transport to industrial innovation, the state shapes the systems and incentives that determine public behaviour and business performance.

premium

Public infrastructure and civic services reflect the role of the state in shaping everyday life. Debashis Basu argues that persistent failures in public behaviour and business performance often stem from weak institutions and governance. | Image : sbmurban.org

Debashis Basu5 min read Last Updated : Nov 01 2026 | 10:28 PM ISTWhen something goes wrong in a country, the usual instinct is to blame the people involved. If streets are filthy, citizens “have no civic sense”. If companies spend too little on research, businessmen are “short-sighted”. If drivers kill pedestrians, motorists are “reckless”. “What can the government do” goes the refrain these days. There is usually some truth in these accusations. But the deeper truth is that behaviour does not exist independent of the environment in which people make decisions. Citizens operate within systems of incentives, infrastructure, rules, enforcement, and expectations. Note that these are shaped by the state. An individual behavioural problem is the final manifestation of an institutional failure much further upstream.  Modern economies are not spontaneous collections of virtuous citizens and entrepreneurial firms. They are organised systems. The role of a capable state is to create conditions in which millions of private decisions produce useful outcomes. Singapore’s extraordinary cleanliness is often attributed to a culture of discipline, but that reverses cause and effect. Singapore’s government spent decades building drainage, sewerage, waste collection, and disposal systems while combining public education with strict enforcement. Repeated enforcement and reliable public services created expectations about what public behaviour should look like, and those expectations eventually became part of the culture. No country simply discovered a population with an unusually large supply of civic virtue. Institutions helped produce the behaviour that outsiders later described as culture.  The Swachh Bharat Mission demonstrated that government spending can accelerate toilet construction on a huge scale, but without water, maintenance, sewage treatment, waste collection, and municipal systems, the citizen is asked to complete a chain that begins and ends with government infrastructure. South Korea, Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand made rapid progress in sanitation not merely by persuading individuals to change their habits but by treating sanitation as a public-health and infrastructure problem.  Under Singapore’s public-housing system, the government assembled land, planned towns, built millions of homes, and integrated transport, schools, and amenities. The state effectively created an urban ecosystem in which the private economy could operate. Yet Singapore is hardly a socialist economy. It is one of the world’s most business-friendly places. India made exactly the opposite choices, which is why we are paying exorbitant prices for property while businesses remain tied up in red tape. Singaporeans did not possess a special genetic preference for public transport. The government built a reliable, integrated system, and used land-use planning and policies affecting car ownership and usage to make public transport an attractive choice.  It is easy to say that India’s roads are dangerous because Indian drivers are undisciplined. Sweden’s Vision Zero approach starts from a more useful assumption: Human beings everywhere make mistakes, so the transport system must be designed to ensure that mistakes do not automatically become deaths. This means road engineering, speed management, pedestrian protection, vehicle standards, licensing, and enforcement matter alongside driver behaviour. Think of standards, an invisible foundation of modern societies. Citizens rely on standards for food safety, vehicle safety, accounting, buildings, medicines, and financial institutions. The state creates this trust infrastructure, allowing strangers to transact at scale.  Governments and commentators routinely complain that Indian businesses spend too little on research & development (R&D). R&D is expensive, uncertain, and slow to pay off; knowledge spills over to competitors. Skilled researchers may be scarce; universities may be poorly connected to industry; and an established technology can often be bought more cheaply than a new one can be developed. Telling companies to become more innovative does nothing to change those incentives. The United States is celebrated for private-sector innovation, but hidden from the public view are decades of public investment in basic science, defence research, universities, and procurement. From this emerged the internet, the Global Positioning System (GPS), semiconductors, and many technologies subsequently commercialised by private firms.  After the Meiji Restoration in the 19th century, Japan recognised that a country starting far behind the industrial powers could not simply wait for private capital and entrepreneurial culture to catch up. It imported technology, built infrastructure, established technical education, and created institutions capable of absorbing foreign knowledge. After the Second World War, the relationship between government and industry became more sophisticated. The government coordinated with companies on technology, finance, standards, and exports, while Japanese firms competed fiercely in international markets.  In South Korea, the government did not simply exhort Samsung, Hyundai, and other companies to become world-class. It built infrastructure, expanded technical education, directed finance, encouraged exports, and linked industrial policy to national development. State support was used to force them to become globally competitive. The bureaucracy had to be close enough to business to understand its problems while retaining enough autonomy to withdraw support from failed activities. The combination — sometimes described as embedded autonomy — is more important than the simple presence of industrial policy. China represents the largest experiment ever in embedded autonomy. Its electric-vehicle industry emerged from a directed process in which public policy supported battery technology, charging infrastructure, procurement, and manufacturing, while local governments competed fiercely to attract investment.  So, if something persistently goes wrong in a country, we should stop looking at the bottom to blame and look upwards instead. When self-serving, incompetent, or corrupt netas and babus run the country, blaming citizens and companies is not just bad analysis. It is a free pass to the very people who should be held responsible for making things better.

entry.title: Time to revisit Narasimham report
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Time to revisit Narasimham reportTime to revisit Narasimham report

There are multiple reforms that could be undertaken in the banking sector, including reform of state-owned banks, without necessarily privatising them

premium

An assessment of the 1991 Narasimham Committee report highlights unfinished banking reforms, including greater autonomy for public-sector banks, governance changes and a sharper priority-sector lending framework. | Illustration: Ajaya Kumar Mohanty

M S Sriram6 min read Last Updated : Nov 01 2026 | 10:19 PM ISTIt has been 35 years since the Committee on the Financial System (Narasimham Committee) submitted its report in November 1991. This report was called Narasimham I because another committee under M Narasimham on banking-sector reforms submitted its report in 1998, referred to as Narasimham II.  The report makes an interesting read. It is difficult to find fault with its recommendations, even with the hindsight of 35 years. The report has a road map for the financial sector. Many recommendations took years to implement, and many are unfinished.  The committee had some 40 proposals for the reform.  The main recommendations were aimed at taking the Indian banking system towards global standards of capitalisation, accounting, governance, and supervision. Surprisingly the report did not suggest privatising state-owned banks but vehemently advocated professional management insulated from state (departmental) interference. They argued that governance systems should be decoupled from ownership and the strategy should be driven professionally rather than bureaucratically. It went to the extent of indicating that the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) should not have a nominee on bank boards and the state should have only one representative to represent its proprietary interests (two members of the committee wrote a dissent on this, suggesting that there should be no representative of the state, and those should be governed as fully autonomous institutions; they even went to the extent of suggesting that the banking division of the Ministry of Finance should be abolished!).  The committee recommended a separate settlement process for sticky loans. The Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest (Sarfeisi) Act came more than 10 years later in 2002. It suggested that sticky loans be transferred to an asset-reconstruction fund and a separate mechanism be created to recover sticky assets. The first asset-reconstruction company, Arcil, started operating in 2003. It recommended capital-adequacy requirements be on a par with the recommendations of the Bank for International Settlements, which was eventually implemented. But what is interesting are the recommendations of the committee yet to be implemented or are still in the works. They seem to be relevant today.  The committee recommended that the Indian banking sector should consolidate with having three-four large banks (including State Bank of India) and 8-10 national banks. The large banks were expected to be international in nature. The committee even suggested that the international presence of state-owned banks be consolidated into one or two entities so that there could be a substantial global footprint that the world would reckon. While we are increasingly inviting international players to the country, and with greater vigour, the internationalisation of Indian banks has not happened to the extent that the committee recommended. State Bank of India and Bank of Baroda have some international presence, but is that significant enough?  On the issue of consolidation to have 8-10 national banks, we have achieved it, but not through sequencing that the committee suggested and therefore this consolidation may have been a suboptimal exercise. The committee advocated the process be market-determined and organic, the pre-condition being autonomy to state-owned banks. That has not happened.  The committee had an interesting formulation on rural banking. It suggested that rural operations of each of the banks be hived off into a wholly owned subsidiary and the regional rural banks (RRBs) be consolidated into that subsidiary of the sponsor bank. What we have instead is status quo ex-ante with state-owned banks and a consolidation of multiple RRBs into a single RRB under the one-state-one-RRB formula.  The committee recommended ending directed lending; and reducing priority-sector lending targets to 10 per cent with a narrow definition, consisting of small and marginal farmers, artisans, micro enterprises, and small transport operators. The suggestion was that the achievement of priority-sector targets should be reckoned after considering the portfolio of the bank and its rural subsidiary.  It is fascinating that the Narasimham committee was so forward-looking. We have not been able to come to terms with some of the obvious recommendations. There are multiple reforms that could be undertaken in the banking sector, including reform of state-owned banks, without necessarily privatising them. Here are the points of unfinished agenda of the 1991:  1. Governance reform of state-owned banks should start by repealing the Bank Nationalisation Act and getting these under the Companies Act. This is an easy and important step. The banks then will then be governed within the ambit of the Companies Act and the listing norms of the Securities and Exchange Board of India, and will make direct intervention by the ministry a bit more difficult.  2. However, the idea of fully owned subsidiaries of banks to carry out specialised rural activities may be an idea worth testing.  As banks have their insurance and asset-management subsidiaries, it may be a good idea to think of a low-cost no-frill subsidiary for rural operations. Many commercial banks having acquired microfinance institutions have surrendered the licence for their non-banking finance company and are operating those as business correspondents for acquiring inclusive clients in an inexpensive format. Having a rural bank as a subsidiary may be a good idea. It would be similar to asset-management and insurance subsidiaries that the banks run.  3. The priority-sector targets at 40 per cent have remained with a wide and liberal definition where it is possible to achieve all its targets including agriculture without issuing a single kisan card or making a crop loan – taking shelter under the broad definition which includes tractors, farm implements, dairying, fisheries and poultry. This part needs to be sharply defined, with reasonable but stiff targets. Considering the current requirements, a 20 per cent target sharply defined between small and marginal farmers and micro enterprises may be adequate.  It may be a good idea to have a compulsory annual reading of the Narasimham committee report for the brass in the Department of Financial Services and the RBI to remind them of the unfinished agenda of reform. 
 The writer is professor, Centre for Public Policy, Indian Institute of Management Bangalore   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Insurance cheque sent by post: Which date matters?
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Insurance cheque sent by post: Which date matters?Insurance cheque sent by post: Which date matters?

Should the premium be deemed received when the insurer receives the cheque, or when the cheque clears and the proceeds reach its account?

premium

The Supreme Court also observed that in Byles on Bills, 20th Edition, the legal position had been summarised pithily as: “A cheque, unless dishonoured, is payment.” (Photo: Shutterstock)

Jehangir B Gai3 min read Last Updated : Nov 01 2026 | 10:04 PM ISTIn my previous column, I had advised sending the cheque by registered or speed post for payment of premium. When a cheque is sent in this manner, what would be the date of receipt of premium under the law? Would it be the date when the cheque was dispatched, or the date when the cheque was received by the insurer, or the date when the cheque is encashed and the proceeds credited to the account of the insurer?   There have been several instances, when the insurer takes time to deposit the cheque promptly before the expiry of the existing policy. If an accident occurs during the window period between the time when the cheque is received and the date on which it is deposited, would the renewed insurance policy be considered to be valid?  The insurer always relies on Section 64VB of the Insurance Act which mandates that no insurance company can assume any risk unless the premium has been received in advance. On the basis of this clause, the insurer takes the stand that in the absence of the premium being credited to its account, it would not be liable for any claim occurring during this window period. So the claim is rejected due to non-compliance with the statutory requirement under Section 64VB of the Insurance Act. Even courts have upheld such rejection by interpreting this provision of Section 64VB in isolation. Is such an interpretation correct, or is there a way out?  The crux of the dispute is the date on which the premium should be considered as having been received. Should the date of its receipt be considered to be the date, or should it be the date when the amount was realised by the insurer? If the date of receipt is considered to be the date of receipt of the cheque by the insurer regardless of the date when it is presented for encashment, what would happen if the cheque gets dishonoured later? How is the date of receipt to be interpreted?  This issue about which date should be considered as the date of payment when a cheque is issued has been decided in a landmark but seldom used ruling of the Supreme Court in the case of The Commissioner of Income Tax, South Bombay v/s Ogale Glass Works.  While deciding the matter, the Supreme Court noted the judgment delivered by Lord Maugham in Bhokana Corporation v/s Inland Revenue Commissioner that common law considers that when payment is made by cheque which is subject to realisation, the date when it was posted would be considered as the date of payment, except in the case of subsequent dishonour.  The Supreme Court also observed that in Byles on Bills, 20th Edition, the legal position had been summarised pithily as: “A cheque, unless dishonoured, is payment.”  The Supreme Court, therefore, concluded that when a cheque is not dishonoured, but has been encashed and payment realised, the date of payment would relate back to the date of receipt of the cheque.  Hence, when submitting a cheque, it is necessary to retain a photocopy   of the signed cheque to ensure that the insurer does not tamper with or alter it   later to wilfully get it dishonoured. Delivery of the cheque in time is sufficient to make the insurer liable for renewal of the policy with continuity and without break.

entry.title: AI could be the force multiplier PSBs need
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / AI could be the force multiplier PSBs needAI could be the force multiplier PSBs need

The technology can transform public-sector banks, driving massive productivity, inclusion and helping in sustained economic growth

premium

public sector bank, artificial intelligence, Banking

Pratik Shah4 min read Last Updated : Nov 01 2026 | 9:41 PM ISTIndia’s ambition to become a $30 trillion economy by 2047 will require its banking sector to operate at a vastly different scale. As the economy expands, banking assets may need to grow 12-14 times. For public-sector banks (PSBs), this could mean sustaining asset growth of around 13.5 per cent annually for the next two decades.  AI agenda: However, scale alone will not suffice. PSBs will need to serve a fundamentally different customer, extend profitable banking deeper into Bharat and preserve the trust built over decades. Artificial intelligence (AI) may well be the force multiplier that enables the reinvention of public-sector banking.  The opportunity is larger than deploying chatbots or automating isolated processes. There is a need for a distinct “PSB.AI” agenda which brings together five connected shifts: Primacy, smart capacity, Bharat impact, augmented workforce, and integrity and trust. AI is one of the few capabilities capable of moving all five simultaneously.  Customer primacy: Banking is entering a new demographic era. By 2035, Gen Z is expected to account for nearly 47 per cent of our workforce and drive $2 trillion in consumer spending. This generation expects banking to be personalised, responsive, transparent and always available. AI can connect signals dispersed across transactions, service interactions, digital journeys and relationship-manager conversations to create a continuously evolving understanding of customer needs.  Productivity equation: Our analysis suggests that supporting India’s long-term growth could require a six-to-eight-fold increase in employee productivity across PSBs. Simply adding people and processes in proportion to balance-sheet growth is unlikely to be sustainable. AI can enable banks to redesign work itself. Standardised activities can be automated, analytical work can be AI-assisted, whereas judgement-intensive decisions can remain with experienced officers. In lending, agentic AI can support everything from lead generation to underwriting and disbursement, releasing between 60 and 80 per cent capacity for relationship managers and officers.  Augmenting people: With more than 90 per cent of PSB employees operating in branches, workforce transformation will be critical. The opportunity is not to substitute human judgement but to amplify it. AI can provide employees with customer context, policy guidance, knowledge support and decision assistance exactly when needed. New joiners can become productive faster; officers can carry context across geographies and relationship managers can engage customers more holistically.  India’s next bankable customer may not always resemble yesterday’s borrower. Gig workers, creators, women entrepreneurs, farmers and micro-businesses often remain outside conventional lending frameworks despite having viable economics. AI can help bridge this gap through cashflow data, UPI activity, alternative data and behavioural signals. Equally important, AI can improve the economics of serving dispersed and smaller-ticket customers through lower servicing costs and smarter collections.  Architecture of trust: For PSBs, the cost of failure is not merely a technology issue; it risks eroding trust built over decades. Trust, therefore, cannot be added after deployment. It must be designed into AI systems through accountability, governance, explainability and continuous monitoring. Institutions that scale AI successfully will be those that move quickly without compromising control.  Realising the PSB.AI agenda requires more than use cases. Banks will need a business-owned AI strategy, operating models built for scale, modern technology architecture, AI-ready data and governance frameworks that balance innovation with control. Success will depend as much on organisational choices as technology choices. AI must move from scattered experimentation to enterprise-wide value creation.  If India is to build a $30 trillion economy by 2047, it will need financial institutions capable of matching that ambition. For PSBs, AI offers an opportunity — not simply to become larger banks, but better ones: More productive, more inclusive, more customer-centric and more resilient. Those that move fastest will not just participate in India’s growth story. They will help define the future of banking itself.

entry.title: Fundamental factors
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Fundamental factorsFundamental factors

FPI taxation and capital flows should not be mixed

premium

FPIs this year net sold Indian stocks worth about ₹2.9 trillion and were net sellers in 2025 too

Business Standard Editorial Comment4 min read Last Updated : Nov 03 2026 | 10:06 PM ISTDespite the recent pullback in equity markets, considerable anxiety exists among retail investors, including those investing through mutual funds in a disciplined manner using systematic investment plans. The benchmark Nifty 50 is down about 9 per cent since the beginning of this year and is flat since January 2025. Persistent selling by foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) is one reason for this underperformance.  FPIs this year net sold Indian stocks worth about ₹2.9 trillion and were net sellers in 2025 too. This has led to demands that taxes on them should be reconsidered. The argument is that most jurisdictions don’t tax foreign investors, which tends to affect the capital-allocation decisions of large international fund managers.  In this context, Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, during an interaction this week, acknowledged the concern over sustained FPI selling. However, the minister rightly pointed out that the tax structure was the same when India received robust capital inflows in 2023-24. No changes had been made to attract capital flows. She did acknowledge that the circumstances had changed since then. It has been reported that the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) has also recommended removing long-term capital gains (LTCG) tax imposed on foreign investors. Given that the tax is not affecting market functioning in any manner, it is intriguing why Sebi is making such suggestions. Perhaps the market regulator is conveying its gleanings from conversations with FPIs and stakeholders. Be that as it may, the issue is worth debating. The outflow clearly has not happened because of taxes. It is worth highlighting that FPIs are buying too — it is just that the amount of selling is higher in the aggregate. For instance, FPIs have been net buyers thus far in November’s two days of trading, and were net buyers through July and August.  For policy purposes, the issue of recent FPI flows must be separated from that of taxation. Outflows are being driven by more fundamental factors, with implications for macroeconomic management. Risk capital from across the world is being invested in a big way in artificial intelligence (AI) and related areas. Since India is not a large player in AI, it is finding it difficult to attract foreign capital. The other reason is the significant increase in government bond yields across the world. An increase in the risk-free rate tends to push up the asking rate of return for other assets. These, along with higher oil prices owing to the conflict in West Asia, are putting pressure on the balance of payments and, consequently, the rupee.  Thus, the macroeconomic response to the situation needs to be much wider. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) attracted foreign flows under swap schemes, including one for Non-Resident Indians. The data suggests that it is using its reserves to contain the decline in the rupee. The RBI has also put various restrictions in the currency-derivatives market to curb volatility. However, these measures will work if global conditions are expected to turn favourable soon. If the underlying conditions persist for a few more months, macroeconomic management could become more challenging. A lot will depend on how the results of the midterm elections in the United States influence its actions in West Asia. On the issue of taxation, since India needs robust capital flows in all circumstances to supplement domestic savings to achieve higher economic growth, its policies should not be out of sync with the rest of the world. The government will have to consider various other aspects, such as taxing different instruments for resident investors. Ideally, differential tax treatment should not influence investment decisions unless that is the desired policy objective.     Topics : FPI outflow Foreign Portfolio Investors LTCG tax Nifty 50 Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: A trust deficit
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / A trust deficitA trust deficit

Govt must respect arbitral awards

premium

The Supreme Court of India, which heard the long-running arbitration dispute involving the government and Vedanta

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 03 2026 | 10:18 PM ISTThe Supreme Court has succinctly articulated a key impediment to a vibrant investment climate in India: The Government of India’s consistent refusal to honour arbitral awards. The court was hearing a 22-year-old dispute in which the government was challenging an arbitral award — for a third time — in a production-sharing contract with a consortium to develop oil and gas fields in the Krishna-Godavari basin. The arbitration, which began in 2004, has had a tortuous journey through an arbitration panel award to Vedanta (then Cairn Energy) and Ravva Oil (Singapore) in Kuala Lumpur, unsuccessful appeals in the Malaysian courts, a $99 million demand from the government, a second round of litigation in Malaysia, rejection by the Delhi High Court in 2026, and finally, a Supreme Court appeal. The two-judge Bench of Justice J B Pardiwala and Justice Manmohan pointed to the Centre’s practice of contesting the enforcement of the arbitration award after decades of litigation. They pointed out “no one would trust the government” if it persisted with such practices.  The issue of trust is intrinsic to international commerce. Yet the government’s maximalist legal approach or its penchant for leveraging its policymaking powers to elude contractual arbitration awards has become a sticking point in concluding bilateral investment treaties (BITs) or in India’s emergence as a credible arbitration centre. In 2012, for instance, the Manmohan Singh government passed a law taxing, with retrospective effect, overseas deals involving Indian corporations. The law triggered international arbitration for Vodafone’s acquisition of Hutchison’s share in Hutchison Essar and a corporate reorganisation for Cairn Energy in India, both of which the government lost but declined to honour.  Then followed embarrassing developments as Cairn moved to seize Indian state assets in France and the United Kingdom to enforce the award, after which the retrospective tax law was scrapped in 2021. But the fact that the Narendra Modi government terminated most of the BITs in 2016, including with major trading partners, underlined New Delhi’s inherent intransigence to international arbitration. Since then, the replacement Model BIT introduced a five-year exhaustion clause of local remedies. The policy yielded BITs with a handful of mostly marginal countries. This encouraged the government to soften its approach. The 2024 BITs with the United Arab Emirates is reported to have reduced the local-remedy clause to three years and the one with Saudi Arabia had a two-year stipulation. Trading partners have sought a one-year clause, which New Delhi has not accepted so far.  The government remains an energetic litigator against arbitral awards, accounting for more than 40 per cent of the challenges against those filed before the Delhi High Court between 2021 and 2024, according to a study. The government has admitted in Parliament that state-owned power and road corporations accounted for more than 60 per cent of the challenges. Given this record and the snail-paced functioning of the judicial system, it is no surprise that long-drawn efforts to establish India as a major arbitration hub have gone nowhere, despite legislative amendments to facilitate a faster enforcement of arbitral awards. Investors are likely to weigh these developments against the government’s persistent evasive proclivities. The Cairn-Ravva saga does not enhance confidence in the government as a business partner or predictable policymaker.     Topics : Supreme Court Arbitration International Arbitration Centre Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Shifts in labour market
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Shifts in labour marketShifts in labour market

India must prepare for greater AI adoption

premium

Artificial intelligence is reshaping workplace roles, increasing demand for new skills and changing employment prospects (Photo: Reuters)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 02 2026 | 10:32 PM ISTArtificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the nature of work and is raising questions about the future of employment, particularly in economies with large and growing workforces. The traditional pathway of moving workers from agriculture to manufacturing and services is becoming harder to sustain as production becomes more capital- and technology-intensive. As a mid-size information-technology (IT) company told this newspaper, the role of entry-level engineers is collapsing because of AI. In this regard, a study in the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF’s) latest “Regional Economic Outlook” for Asia and Pacific provides an early assessment of the shift. Drawing on 40 million online job postings across 19 Asian economies, it finds that employer demand in occupations more exposed to AI has fallen by nearly 10 per cent since the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022. While this decline has stabilised despite rapid improvement in AI capabilities, the report cautions against interpreting this as evidence that displacement risks have receded. The effects of reduced hiring are likely to unfold only over time.   There are, however, emerging opportunities. Demand is increasing for workers with skills in prompt engineering, retrieval-augmented generation, and AI agent development. However, only about 6 per cent of firms in Asia seek explicit AI skills in their job postings. The study finds that hiring demand is growing faster at firms adopting AI, including for occupations highly exposed to the technology. This suggests that AI can complement workers by raising their productivity, even as it substitutes for certain tasks. The challenge is ensuring that the new opportunities are sufficiently broad to offset the reduction in conventional hiring. The implications differ across economies. Ageing countries such as Japan and South Korea could use AI to mitigate shrinking workforces. For India, Indonesia and the Philippines, which have expanding working-age populations, the challenge involves creating enough productive employment to harness their demographic dividends. These economies are now partly shielded because large numbers of workers remain in agriculture, a sector less exposed to AI. However, development requires a shift towards higher-productivity manufacturing and services, precisely where AI could make job creation more difficult.  Notably, high unemployment among the youth, skill mismatches among graduates, and widespread underemployment already constrain employment prospects across emerging Asia. The IMF’s analysis of 65 million career histories finds that only about 5 per cent of workers move across occupations annually. This underlines why reskilling cannot be treated as an automatic solution to technological displacement. Workers need accessible training, institutional support, and opportunities to transition into occupations where demand is growing. India must, therefore, rethink its approach to employment generation and workforce preparedness. Education systems need to move beyond conventional qualifications towards adaptable, technology-oriented skills. Equally important is the direction of technological adoption. If AI-driven gains accrue disproportionately to a handful of firms, taxation and welfare policies may have to be revisited. For countries such as India, ensuring access to frontier AI technologies while building domestic capabilities in infrastructure, data and expertise will be equally important.   Topics : Artificial intelligence Employment Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Insalubrious climate for reform
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Insalubrious climate for reformInsalubrious climate for reform

COP31 is up against all-round failures

premium

World leaders to gather in Antalya, Turkey, for the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) (Photo: Website)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 02 2026 | 10:18 PM ISTNext week, leaders of 90 countries will converge in the salubrious “Turkish Riviera” town of Antalya for the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (called Conference of Parties 31, or COP31). However, the idyllic setting is not expected to yield much good news. It is already clear that the 2015 Paris agreement target to hold increases in global average temperatures below 1.5 to 2 degrees centigrade above pre-industrial levels is unlikely to materialise. In November last year, the United Nations Environment Programme’s “Emissions Gap” report suggested that global temperatures would breach the lower threshold of 1.5 degrees centigrade within the next decade, far faster than climate advocates had hoped, thanks to accelerated fossil-fuel burning. The report points out that there is more carbon dioxide in the atmosphere than at any point in the last two million years. So even if countries lived up to their Nationally Determined Contributions — and the report is doubtful on this score — the world will warm by 2.3 to 2.5 degrees centigrade by the end of the century.  Faced with this disastrous scenario, the effort in Antalya is to limit peak warming to a “low overshoot path” of 1.7-1.8 degrees centigrade before cooling to 1.5 degrees centigrade in 2100. This will require considerably higher emission-cutback pledges than those made in Paris; given that the world has already warmed 1.44 degrees centigrade above pre-industrial levels, only an unalloyed optimist can hope to reach those targets. Beyond unchecked fossil-fuel burning is the sustained reluctance of the developed world, which is responsible for global warming in the first place, to underwrite urgently needed mitigation and adaptation projects in the climate change-impacted poor and developing world. The United States’ repudiation of the Paris Agreement set the trend in Donald Trump's first term as President and his second stint saw the mass exit of private finance from climate-funding initiatives.  Much has been made of the fact that climate finance has crossed $2 billion annually. But this amount lags annual requirements of $7.8 trillion till 2030. The bulk of this meagre finance goes into mitigation projects (such as renewable energy and emission reduction) that have revenue-earning potential, leaving little for adaptation programmes (such as infrastructure to contain sea-level rises) needed in scores of island-nations and countries with long coastlines. Climate-finance meetings ahead of Antalya did not suggest a fundamental alteration of this funding paradigm or amount.  India has consistently outperformed its Paris Agreement commitments. It exceeded its non-fossil-fuel electric-power target nine years ahead of schedule and its emission intensity reduction 10 years ahead, and is on track to create an additional carbon sink. This track record has given New Delhi the confidence to set challenging targets for Nationally Determined Contribution for 2031 to 2035. These are creditable achievements that also go a long way towards reducing India’s fossil-fuel dependence. But these developments must be weighed against steady ecological destruction, which also plays a role in climate change. Diminishing biodiversity in the Western Ghats and other Indian forests for mining and commercial plantations, for example, unchecked construction in the Aravallis, the indiscriminate building of dams and railways in fragile terrain in Arunachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, and the disastrous pollution of the oceans are all trajectories that will eventually annul the achievements of the Paris targets. They, too, need to be addressed with the same urgency as emission norms.   Topics : Climate Change Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment Global Warming Paris agreement

entry.title: Go beyond banking
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Go beyond bankingGo beyond banking

An efficient financial structure will support growth

premium

The Union government has set up a high-level committee headed by former central vigilance commissioner Suresh N Patel to review India's banking sector and recommend reforms to make it more competitive, inclusive and resilient.

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 01 2026 | 11:18 PM ISTThe Union government last week constituted a high-level committee to review the state of India’s banking sector and recommend regulatory, structural, institutional, and legislative reforms to make it globally competitive, inclusive, and resilient to be able to meet the needs of a developed country by 2047. The committee’s constitution follows an announcement in this year’s Union Budget. The committee, headed by former central vigilance commissioner Suresh N Patel, according to the terms of reference (ToR), will be expected to look into areas such as banking practices and prudential norms, existing regulatory and legal frameworks, issues related to capital requirements (including for development finance institutions and non-bank financial companies), and the priority-sector lending (PSL) framework, and prepare a road map for artificial intelligence and digital innovation in banking.  Any exercise that assesses the current position and examines possibilities, along with the supporting regulatory and legal framework, must be welcomed. India is seen as a largely bank-financed economy, and an efficient banking system will help channelise savings into real investment. The committee’s ToR are also fairly comprehensive. While it will look into various aspects of banking, its observations on specific issues will be keenly awaited. India has a mix of public-sector banks (PSBs), private banks, regional rural banks, cooperative banks, new-age payments banks and small-finance banks, which makes the sector fairly vibrant. Nevertheless, estimates suggest that there is large unmet demand for credit. A 2025 NITI Aayog report, for instance, noted that only 19 per cent of credit demand among micro, small and medium enterprises was met through formal sources in 2020-21.  In fact, this could be a good starting point for the committee. Why does India have large unmet credit demand?  It would also be worth probing whether India needs so many PSBs in this day and age. It must be remembered that the Union government had to undertake a massive capital infusion into PSBs in the aftermath of the global financial crisis. There has also been a debate on different regulatory standards for PSBs. In fact, there is a case for improved and transparent regulations in general. For instance, the chairman of a large private bank abruptly resigned earlier this year, citing governance and ethical issues. It is still not known what exactly the issues were. Given that large banks can pose systemic risks, such occurrences cannot be allowed. Further, the committee will look into the much-debated issue of the PSL framework. Many, including officials in the government, say that the framework needs to be adjusted. There is no need to expect all banks to do the same kind of things. It is also hoped that the committee will undertake a comprehensive review of regulatory requirements, including those related to the maintenance of the statutory liquidity ratio. In the interests of transparency in a market-driven economy, is there a case for progressively reducing such requirements? Are such requirements affecting interest in the banking sector?  While the committee will look into these issues, it is worth highlighting that banks are only one part of the broader financial system. In a large, growing, and complex economy, financing requirements will be met by different kinds of providers and instruments. Thus, there is a need to holistically review the functioning of the Indian financial sector. Nevertheless, the high-level banking committee is a step in the right direction. The government must broaden its scope and review all aspects of the Indian economy to chart a course towards making India a developed country.

entry.title: AI capex boom
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / AI capex boomAI capex boom

Global tech investors are evaluating returns

premium

Heavy spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure has raised concerns among investors about funding requirements, cash flows and the returns from Big Tech's AI investments. (Photo: Reuetrs)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 01 2026 | 10:05 PM ISTFour tech giants — Google, Meta, Amazon, and Microsoft — lost an aggregate $900 billion in market value last Thursday after declaring their respective third-quarter (July-September 2026) results. On Friday, big tech shares continued to slide. The biggest loser was Alphabet, Google’s parent, which had its market capitalisation shaved off by $500 billion with a catastrophic 13 per cent drop in one session. Amazon lost 7 per cent and Meta 6 per cent. All of these companies continue to be highly profitable but disappointed the street. The cited rationales for the selloffs are interesting. The bearish sentiment is centred, one way or another, on exposure to artificial intelligence (AI).  Google’s search business is being cannibalised by its own AI model, Gemini. Search and other revenues grew 12 per cent year-on-year to $63.35 billion, much lower than the 17 per cent growth in Q2 and 19 per cent in Q1. Alphabet’s capital expenditure (capex) in the quarter was $51.4 billion, which was more than double that in the same quarter last year. Google’s free cash flow fell to a negative $9.1 billion from a positive $24.5 billion a year ago. This was only the second quarter of negative cash flow since it went public in 2004. Google also reported a second successive quarter of slowing growth in search revenues, and admitted that its increase in ad revenues had eased because users had moved to using the overviews generated by the Gemini chatbot rather than relying on traditional search with its pages of links. Users who saw an AI summary clicked through for links on only 8 per cent of visits. Google is starting to put more ads in Gemini overviews in order to compensate.  The other big losers, Amazon and Meta, have seen downgrades because they too have spent more money on AI-related investment than investors are comfortable with. Google, Meta and Amazon all registered negative cash flow because of the sheer scale of their AI-related investment. Microsoft is the only one that has reported positive cash flow. Analysts calculated that the four tech giants’ AI-related capex in Q3 was $207 billion as against $113 billion spent by them during the same period last year. Collective guidance is for AI-related capex to the tune of another $232 billion in Q4 and close to $750 billion in aggregate for the full year. Capex has hit levels where even four highly profitable companies cannot fund it through internal accruals. Alphabet has raised debt and plans to mobilise $85 billion through an equity issue. Meta is looking at an equity funding of $95 billion.  AI expenditure is paying off. Google Cloud’s revenues more than doubled, up 103 per cent to $30.71 billion. Amazon Web Services saw a 39 per cent rise in Cloud sales to $46 billion. Google also has many inquiries for its tensor processing unit AI chips, which, according to reports, could generate $75 billion in 2027 sales. According to the company, there is more demand for its data centres than it can satisfy. The unrestrained capex has led to concerns about the stresses involved in funding the AI boom. The bearish market response cast doubts on the sustainability of AI investment in a week when Anthropic published its initial public-offering prospectus. For the first time since ChatGPT was launched in November 2022, investors in AI are looking at the cost of capital versus the return on capital employed.   Topics : Google artifical intelligence Capex spending big tech BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Company News Amazon
